metaDescription: Six dual fuel generators ranked for running an RV on propane: output on propane versus gasoline, runtime on a cylinder, regulator upkeep and storage.
expertTake: The WEN 4800 is our top pick for propane-first RV use because it keeps 4,000 rated watts on propane, the best retention in the lineup. The Westinghouse 4650 is the value pick with a strong propane figure and a four gallon gas backup. If you never carry a separate propane bottle, a gasoline-only unit is simpler.
introParagraphs: Propane is the fuel an RV already knows how to carry. It stores for years, burns clean and avoids the stale gasoline that ruins small carburetors, which is why many owners want a generator that treats it as the main fuel rather than a backup.

The catch is that propane is less energy dense, so every machine loses some output, and the loss varies a lot between models. The useful comparison is how many watts each one still delivers on propane, how long a cylinder lasts and how the regulator and hose are built.

products.name: WEN 4800 Watt Dual Fuel RV Ready Inverter, Electric Start
products.description:
The headline here is that the rated watts do not move: 4,000 on gasoline and 4,000 on propane, with only the surge number falling from 4,800 to 4,320. For a propane-first owner, that means the full continuous capacity is available from the bottle, so an air conditioner and a microwave do not force a switch to gasoline.

The 224cc dual fuel engine and electric start suit a coach with a large propane supply. Electric start matters on propane, since cold propane vaporizes poorly and a hard pull on a recoil is a real nuisance in cold weather. It is an inverter, so the output is clean and the engine throttles with load.

Ownership is about the regulator and the hose. Check the hose for cracks before every trip, run on propane every couple of months so the regulator diaphragm stays supple, and keep the starter battery charged. It adds inverter quiet and 760 more rated watts on propane over the Westinghouse 4650, which is the difference between running the air conditioner and the microwave together or not. If you boondock a week at a time, that margin is why owners keep this machine over a cheaper one.
products.bestFor: Propane-first owners who need an air conditioner running from the bottle.
pros: Electric start helps cold propane starts
Inverter output is clean and quieter
cons: Surge drops on propane, so hard starts need care

products.name: Westinghouse 4650 Peak Watt Dual Fuel Generator, 30A Outlet
products.description:
This open-frame Westinghouse holds up well on propane: 3,240 rated watts, only about 10 percent below its 3,600 on gasoline. It keeps the same 4,650 peak on either fuel, which is useful for starting a compressor on propane without help from a soft start kit.

It is the budget way into a propane generator, with a four gallon gasoline tank as a backup and a CO sensor that shuts it down. It is louder than the WEN and has no electric start, so a cold morning on propane takes some pulling.

It arrives with oil, a funnel, a tool kit and a manual, so it is ready quickly. It is cheaper than the WEN 4800 but gives 760 fewer rated watts on propane. Keep the hose fresh and the fuel stable, and wipe the exposed recoil handle and wheel kit hardware dry after wet trips, since an open frame has no enclosure to keep the weather off.
products.bestFor: Budget propane owners who accept noise for a strong propane figure.
pros: Only about 10 percent output loss on propane
CO sensor shuts the engine down
cons: Recoil start is hard in the cold
Open frame is much louder than an inverter

products.name: AIVOLT 4300W Dual Fuel Inverter, 34 Hours on Propane, Remote
products.description:
The number that jumps out is 34 hours on propane at a quarter load, against 11.5 on gasoline. That tells you the machine is built around its propane side, since gas runtime is a third of that. For an owner who wants to run on a cylinder for a long weekend, this is the clearest claim in the guide.

A key fob remote start lets you fire it from the couch, and built-in wheels and a telescoping handle make the 64 pound frame manageable. At 53 dB on the label it is also quiet, though that is at a light load.

As with any runtime claim, a quarter load means lights and chargers, not an air conditioner. Expect a fraction of 34 hours when a roof unit runs. Treat the brand as newer and check the warranty, and keep the propane hose and regulator in good shape.
products.bestFor: Campers who want the longest stated runtime from a propane cylinder.
pros: 34 hours on propane at quarter load
Quiet 53 dB label at light load
cons: Runtime claim is at a light load only
Newer brand with limited support history

products.name: Aceup 4000 Watt Dual Fuel Inverter Generator, 149cc

specList.label: Runtime
specList.value: About 5 hours at half load on 1.32 gallons

specList.label: Noise
specList.value: About 60 dB in Eco at 25% load

products.description:
Aceup's propane loss is small: 3,000 rated watts against 3,200 on gasoline, a drop of only 200 watts. That is a tight spread, and it helps a trailer owner who wants nearly the same capacity on either fuel.

It is a compact inverter with a 149cc engine and a recoil start, which suits a small to mid-size trailer. The 1.32 gallon gas tank claims about five hours at half load, which is modest, so the propane side carries the long runs. A noise level around 60 dB in Eco mode at a quarter load keeps it polite.

It costs less than the WEN 4800 and weighs less, but a 149cc engine at 3,000 watts runs closer to its limit. Change the oil early and clean the filter often, and expect to pay attention to the choke and fuel selector the first few times so you learn how it behaves when you change fuel. On propane it beats the WEN 3600 by about 400 rated watts.
products.bestFor: Small to mid-size trailers that want near-equal output on both fuels.
pros: Propane output only 200 watts below gas
Lower weight than the larger WEN
cons: Small gasoline tank for long gas runs
Engine works near its limit at full load

products.name: WEN 3600 Watt Dual Fuel RV Ready Inverter, Fuel Shutoff
products.description:
On propane this WEN gives 2,600 rated watts, 300 below its gasoline figure, which is a small RV class number. It is the right size for a trailer with one air conditioner and light loads, and it is more comfortable running on propane when you do not stack appliances.

The fuel shutoff valve helps even a propane-first owner, because you can close the valve and burn off the gasoline in the bowl before storage. That prevents gummed jets on the rare occasions you use gasoline.

Compared with the Aceup 4000 it has less output but a stronger brand behind it. Run it on propane every few months, check the regulator and hose, and keep vents clear. Because it is the smallest propane-capable machine in this guide, it also makes a sensible spare for a bigger coach, and its modest draw means a standard cylinder goes a long way.
products.bestFor: Small trailers with one air conditioner that run mainly on propane.
pros: Supported brand with good parts access
cons: 2,600 rated watts on propane is tight with an air conditioner

products.name: DuroMax XP13000EH 13000 Watt Dual Fuel Generator, Electric Start
products.description:
DuroMax is the large machine in this guide, sold as a whole-home backup that also suits a big RV. It runs on propane, which for a stationary or home use means a large tank or a propane supply that can last a long time.

The listing gives a headline of 13,000 watts but not a propane rating, and propane lowers output noticeably, so size the machine from the propane figure in the manual. It is a heavy open frame with electric start, and its engine is a large OHV design.

It does not suit casual weekend campers. For a 50 amp coach with two or three air conditioners, or a house with a transfer switch, it provides ample capacity. Keep the battery charged and run it monthly.
products.bestFor: 50 amp coaches and home backup where propane supply is large.
pros: 13,000 watts on gasoline for heavy loads
cons: No propane rating on the listing

buyingCriteria.explanation: Propane carries less energy than gasoline, so output drops. The WEN 4800 keeps 4,000 rated on both fuels, the Aceup 4000 falls from 3,200 to 3,000, the Westinghouse 4650 from 3,600 to 3,240 and the WEN 3600 from 2,900 to 2,600. Size on the propane number when propane is your main fuel.

A 20 pound cylinder lasts a day at a light load and a few hours at a heavy one. The AIVOLT 4300 claims 34 hours at 25 percent load, which means lights and chargers. Divide any such claim by three or four if a roof air conditioner will run, and plan a spare cylinder or a larger tank. Weigh a cylinder to know how much is left, since a gauge on a 20 pound tank is a rough guide at best, and a cylinder that reads empty mid-evening is the most common propane-generator complaint. Keeping a second full cylinder in a shaded spot beside the machine removes that worry for a modest cost.

The regulator reduces tank pressure to what the carburetor needs, and its diaphragm stiffens when idle. A cracked hose leaks fuel. Inspect both before every trip and replace rubber parts that show hardening. Never use a hose not rated for propane, and keep the regulator on the supplied connection rather than swapping parts, since a mismatched fitting can leak without any smell until the odorant fades.

Propane vaporizes poorly when cold, so starting can be harder in freezing weather. Electric start, as on the WEN 4800 and DuroMax XP13000EH, helps. Recoil units like the Westinghouse 4650 take effort. Store the cylinder in a sheltered spot, not in direct frost, and let a very cold cylinder warm slightly before connecting it, since a frosted tank delivers lower pressure than the carburetor wants.

A dual fuel unit lets you fall back to gasoline when the cylinder is empty. The Westinghouse 4650's four gallon tank is a strong backup, while the Aceup's 1.32 gallons is modest. Automatic switching, offered on some units, avoids a shutdown mid-night, but verify it on the listing before you rely on it, since a unit that does not name the feature will shut down when a cylinder empties.

Propane is heavier than air and pools low, so keep the cylinder upright and outdoors, away from ignition sources. Run the generator in open air, well away from windows. A battery CO detector inside the RV and a propane leak detector are cheap protection. Do not store a spare cylinder inside a living space or a closed bay, and keep any cylinder valve closed whenever the generator is not in use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Propane output retention
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared rated watts on propane against gasoline. The WEN 4800 held steady at 4,000, while the WEN 3600 lost 300 watts and the Westinghouse 4650 lost about 360.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cylinder runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: Published runtimes on propane were compared. The AIVOLT 4300's 34 hours at quarter load led. Claims were treated as light-load figures.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cold starting
howWeEvaluated.description: Electric start was favored for propane use. Recoil units were marked lower for cold weather.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fuel backup
howWeEvaluated.description: Gasoline tank size and switching logic were considered. The Westinghouse 4650's four gallons stood out.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on owner feedback patterns, we weighed regulator and hose upkeep, brand support and parts. WEN and Westinghouse scored well.

cards.label: Inverter (WEN, Aceup, AIVOLT)
cards.text: Quieter, clean power and throttle that follows load, which stretches a cylinder. The WEN 4800 keeps its rating on propane.

cards.label: Open frame (Westinghouse 4650, DuroMax)
cards.text: Cheaper per watt and simpler, but louder and fixed-speed, which burns propane faster at light load.

howToChoose.note: Choose inverter to stretch a cylinder; choose open frame for raw capacity at low cost.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Electric start, a sheltered cylinder and a regulator that tolerates cold. Keep the cylinder at least partly full, since low pressure worsens in freezing air.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WEN 4800 and DuroMax XP13000EH offer electric start. The Westinghouse 4650 has a gasoline backup for the coldest mornings.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want an air conditioner on propane or a quiet inverter. The WEN 4800 earns its cost with 4,000 rated watts on both fuels.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You run light loads or a fridge. The Westinghouse 4650 or Aceup 4000 suffice.

maintenance.why: Rubber hardens and cracks over time. A leak wastes fuel and is a fire risk.
Regulator diaphragms stiffen when idle. A run under load keeps them working.
Propane burns clean but crankcases still collect break-in debris.
Electric start units need a healthy battery, especially in cold weather.
Use soapy water to check for bubbles at fittings, and do it with the cylinder valve open but the engine off, so any leak shows before the machine runs. Replace any worn seals.

faq.q: Is propane better than gasoline for an RV generator?
faq.a: It stores for years and avoids stale fuel, but gives less output. Most owners use propane for convenience and gasoline for maximum power.

faq.q: How long will a 20 pound cylinder last?
faq.a: At a light load a day or more, at a heavy air conditioner load a few hours. The AIVOLT 4300 claims 34 hours at quarter load.

faq.q: Which is the best budget choice?
faq.a: The Westinghouse 4650 is the lowest cost per watt with a strong propane figure. The Aceup 4000 is a compact inverter alternative.

faq.q: Will my generator start in cold weather on propane?
faq.a: Usually, but propane vaporizes slowly in the cold. Electric start helps, and a cylinder kept in a sheltered spot works better.

faq.q: Can I connect to my RV's propane tank?
faq.a: Not without a proper regulator and fittings. The RV system runs at a different pressure. Use a separate cylinder for the generator unless you have a certified setup.

faq.q: Is it safe to run on propane?
faq.a: Yes, when run outdoors and away from windows. Use a propane leak check on connections and a CO detector inside the RV.
